title: Simple universal rules like rule 110 could be built into computers from atoms

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Simple universal rules like rule 110 could be built into computers from atoms

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Since very simple rules such as the rule 110 cellular automaton are universal, computers could be built from many kinds of components, and a simple chemical process could plausibly assemble a rule 110-like computer at the atomic scale, with one or a few atoms per cell.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: For while it is quite implausible that some simple chemical process could successfully assemble a traditional computer out of atoms, it seems quite plausible that this could be done for something like a rule 110 cellular automaton.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 12, “The Principle of Computational Equivalence”; section “Implications for Technology” (from p. 840), p. 841. Scope: molecular and atomic-scale computing technology

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch12-54: needs-new-data, resolvability 0.50

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The proposal has measurable engineering milestones but present public results do not establish the complete device as stated. New fabrication and experimental measurements are required.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Demonstrate a self-assembled molecular or atomic lattice implementing rule-110-equivalent local updates with measured fidelity, scalability, and programmable initial conditions. A functioning construction confirms feasibility; systematic physical constraints can refute specified material implementations but not every possible chemistry.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Universality does not guarantee practical initialization, readout, or error correction.

Plausibility across all chemistries cannot be refuted by one failed implementation.

No existing dataset demonstrates the complete atomic-scale rule-110 computer.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: DNA self-assembly has produced cellular-automaton-like patterns, including Sierpinski triangles, so a chemical medium that carries simple-rule computation is already experimental fact at molecular scale. The sentence specifies a rule 110-like universal computer at one or a few atoms per cell, assembled by a simple chemical process. That object is not in any public dataset, and the coarser demonstrations constrain plausibility only weakly.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Assemble, by a simple chemical process, a lattice whose update is rule 110 or an equivalent universal cellular automaton, with one or a few atoms or molecules per cell, and run a non-trivial computation. Success would confirm the claim. Existing DNA-tile automata confirm a coarser molecular construction.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Plausible and likely have no numerical threshold.

A failed laboratory attempt is compatible with the claim that some simple chemical process could succeed.

DNA tiles show programmed self-assembly of a nested pattern, not a universal computer with one atom per cell.
